hero.headline: Riviera Beach named only Florida city to receive 2026 All-America City Award
hero.teaser: The City of Riviera Beach was named one of just 10 communities in the U.S. to receive the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League and was the only Florida city selected.
hero.body:
Riviera Beach has earned a major national recognition by becoming one of only 10 communities in the United States selected for the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League. The city stands out as the sole Florida municipality to receive this honor this year. The award was announced at the National Civic League conference in Denver, where Riviera Beach leaders presented their work on strengthening community engagement and civic participation.

The All-America City Award recognizes communities that effectively bring together residents, local government, businesses and organizations to address local challenges and create meaningful, lasting change. The award has been presented annually since 1949 and is considered one of the nation's most respected civic honors. Mayor Douglas Lawson expressed pride in the recognition, saying "Little old Riviera Beach is one of the biggest, brightest, shining stars." Lawson noted that the city earned the award through long-term efforts to revitalize the community and improve residents' quality of life. Councilwoman KaShamba Miller-Anderson credited the community for the achievement, stating "This award is a tribute to the heart and determination of our residents. Every event we host, every project we complete, and every challenge we overcome happens because our community shows up for one another."

Riviera Beach's application highlighted several civic engagement programs that demonstrate the city's commitment to community participation. The Riviera Beach Youth Council involves high school students in civic leadership and advocacy work. The Citizens Leadership Academy, a civic education program, has achieved a 98 percent completion rate. The Neighborhood Reclaim Home Rehabilitation Program provides mini-grants to help longtime homeowners make necessary repairs. City leaders emphasized that these programs represent a broader commitment to treating civic engagement as an ongoing partnership between government, residents, faith groups, schools and community organizations. Miller-Anderson noted that the city is "doing a lot of innovative things to make sure that our community is able to say that they are part of what's happening here in the city."

Officials say that being named an All-America City sends a national message that Riviera Beach is a place where collaboration produces results and residents actively shape their community's future. The designation celebrates the city's progress while positioning the community for continued growth and new opportunities. Miller-Anderson added that winning this award reinforces positive momentum and brings back community pride. Other cities receiving the 2026 All-America City Award include Chelsea, Massachusetts; Franklin, Tennessee; Harlingen, Texas; Montgomery, Alabama; Morrisville, North Carolina; Norfolk, Virginia; North Charleston, South Carolina; Roanoke, Virginia; and Woodburn, Oregon.

cards.headline: Florida advances plan to bar undocumented students from state colleges and adult education programs
cards.body:
Florida's State Board of Education has voted to move forward with rules that would prevent undocumented students from enrolling in the state's 28 community colleges and adult education programs. The restrictions would also apply to GED preparation courses, which many students use as a pathway to college or workforce training. This action builds on an earlier decision by Florida's university system Board of Governors, which approved plans to ban undocumented students from the state's more competitive public universities starting in the 2027-28 academic year. Students already enrolled would not be affected by the university proposal.

Those supporting the restrictions contend that taxpayer-funded educational institutions should serve only students who are legally present in the United States. However, immigrant advocates and students have objected strongly to the policy. Alexander Vallejos, a student with DACA protection, argued that Florida is closing opportunities for young people who have lived their entire lives in the state and attended Florida schools. Vallejos stated, "We're just asking for an opportunity to earn our future through education. Because when Dreamers succeed, Florida succeeds." These new restrictions follow Florida's previous decision to eliminate in-state tuition rates for many undocumented students, including those protected under DACA.

The same week, Governor Ron DeSantis began implementing a new state law that enables Florida to designate organizations as terrorist groups. The law, which took effect July 1, allows the governor and Florida Cabinet to make designations based on recommendations from state domestic security officials. DeSantis announced that Florida will seek to designate the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the Muslim Brotherhood, and Antifa, in addition to more than 90 organizations already designated as terrorist groups by the federal government. These federal designations include cartel-connected groups and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

If the Cabinet approves these designations, the state could block taxpayer funding, contracts, and other public support for the listed organizations. The law also imposes penalties for providing material support to designated groups and could allow for dissolution of some organizations under state law. CAIR and civil rights groups immediately filed lawsuits in federal court challenging the designations as unconstitutional. According to a statement from the Southern Poverty Law Center's deputy legal director Scott McCoy, "Gov. DeSantis does not have the power to unilaterally brand an organization with this vilifying designation and punish those who support it without due process or judicial review." Supporters of the law argue that Florida is taking necessary steps to combat extremism and protect public institutions.

cards.headline: Martin County School Board fights judge's order to reinstate teacher suspended over Charlie Kirk comments
cards.teaser: The Martin County School Board filed a court challenge Thursday against a judge's recommendation to reinstate a Spectrum Academy teacher suspended last year aft.
cards.body:
The Martin County School Board is pushing back against a judge's recommendation to reinstate Matt Theobald, a social studies teacher at Spectrum Academy since 2009, who was suspended last year following controversial social media comments about conservative commentator Charlie Kirk. In a Thursday court filing, the school board argued Administrative Law Judge Jodi-Ann Vanessa Livingstone erred in recommending Theobald get his job back, saying "numerous findings ... are not based upon competent substantial evidence." The board's attorney claims Theobald's Facebook post about Kirk, which labeled him as racist, misogynistic and a neo-Nazi, was a "serious offense" and removing him was appropriate.

In an order issued last month, Livingstone cited a recent Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal ruling that said disciplining a teacher for personal Facebook posts made off school grounds, on personal equipment, with no student involvement, violated the teacher's First Amendment rights. The judge also recommended Theobald be awarded back pay and benefits. According to an investigation report, Theobald admitted writing the comments about Kirk but said they were posted on his mother's private Facebook page "within a discussion among personal acquaintances" and were not intended for public view.

cards.headline: Martin County maritime units deploy two boats with medics for Fourth of July boating weekend
cards.teaser: Martin County Maritime Response Unit will have two boats staffed with medics stationed in the north and south areas of the county as hundreds of boaters celebrate the holiday weekend on the water.
cards.body:
Hundreds of boaters are expected to hit the waterways across Florida this Fourth of July weekend. Lt. Brett Harry with Martin County Maritime Response Unit said his team will have two boats with medics on standby in Martin County's north and south regions to assist boaters. "We're just out there to mitigate anybody that needs help, whether it's something as simple as a stubbed toe to anything cardiac related, or potential spinal injuries, or anything like that," Harry said.

Boaters like Brendan and Ashley Shannon launched their boat at Sandsprit Park in Martin County on Friday with their young daughter and puppy, prioritizing safety on the water. Harry emphasized that boaters should keep their eyes on the water, have a designated driver, and pack life vests, whistles and flotation devices. "Just have fun and be safe," Harry said.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds reports raising more than $90 million as Florida GOP governor's race intensifies
cards.teaser: U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds' campaign and affiliated political committee say they have now raised more than $90 million this cycle, including more than $23 million in the second quarter.
cards.body:
Byron Donalds, the front-runner in the GOP race to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis, entered the week with mounting signs of momentum. His campaign and affiliated political committee have raised more than $90 million this cycle, including more than $23 million in the second quarter. The campaign recently launched a $20 million statewide advertising buy, putting Donalds on television as Florida's August primary approaches. Donalds picked up endorsements from Attorney General James Uthmeier and Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia, both statewide officials appointed by DeSantis. He also has backing from the two incoming legislative leaders, Senate President Jim Boyd and House Speaker Sam Garrison. The endorsements are notable in a primary where DeSantis himself has not endorsed a successor, though several figures connected to his administration have lined up behind Donalds.

While Donalds builds money and institutional support, Lt. Gov. Jay Collins filed a lawsuit this week challenging another Republican candidate, James Fishback, arguing he does not meet Florida's constitutional requirement that a governor live in the state for at least seven years before being elected. The legal complaint points to Fishback's ties to Washington, D.C., including allegations that he claimed a D.C. property as a primary residence and voted there in 2020. Fishback has denied the allegations, arguing he was born and raised in Florida and accusing Collins of trying to damage his campaign. The court fight adds another layer of uncertainty to the GOP primary, with mail ballots soon going out and the Aug. 18 primary approaching.

cards.body:
Hundreds of boaters are hitting waterways across Florida to celebrate the Fourth of July weekend. Martin County Maritime Response Unit is deploying two boats with medics on standby in the northern and southern parts of the county to assist boaters during the holiday. Lt. Brett Harry said his team expects hundreds of boaters to be on the water celebrating this weekend.

The maritime response team will handle medical situations ranging from minor injuries like stubbed toes to serious conditions including cardiac events and potential spinal injuries. Harry urged boaters to keep their eyes on the water, have a designated driver, and pack life vests, whistles and flotation devices. Among those taking to the water Friday was the Shannon family, who launched from Sandsprit Park in Martin County with their young daughter and puppy. "Just have fun and be safe," Harry said.

cards.headline: Juno Beach considers replacing fence at JB-7 beach access after condo residents report trespassing
cards.teaser: A missing fence at a Juno Beach public beach access point has created tension between Colony Condos residents and summer beachgoers, and the town may spend thousands of dollars to replace it.
cards.body:
Residents at the Colony Condos are pushing the town to reinstall a fence at the JB-7 public beach access point after the town removed it in 2023 for safety reasons. Since the fence came down, only vegetation separates the public walkway from the condo's private property, and residents say beachgoers are regularly cutting through their land. Lori Hill, a Colony resident, described the summer problem as a recurring issue where visitors park in private spots and push through bushes while carrying coolers, fishing rods, and lawn chairs. Hill said residents initially tried confronting trespassers directly but found many responses became hostile, prompting them to call police instead to handle the situation.

Not all beachgoers acknowledge a significant problem. Michael House, who regularly walks to JB-7 from a nearby public parking lot, said he has not witnessed the trespassing issues residents describe. He suggested that if there are actual property damages or littering, those would be separate concerns worth addressing. House noted that free public parking is available in the area, making it unclear why beachgoers would need to use private condo spaces.

The issue reached the Juno Beach Town Council at a recent meeting, where officials acknowledged the town holds no legal obligation to install a fence. However, Vice Mayor Pro Tem DD Halpern expressed openness to finding solutions and suggested exploring more affordable options than a full replacement fence. Halpern proposed considering a combination approach using split rail fencing paired with landscaping shrubs, which might reduce costs compared to traditional fencing alone. Hill said residents remain hopeful the town will take action to restore clear boundaries between public and private property while protecting their landscaping and parking areas.

The council scheduled the fence question for further discussion during the upcoming budget meetings on July 15, giving town officials time to assess costs and feasibility before making a decision. The dispute highlights the ongoing tension between public beach access and private property rights in the oceanside community, with the resolution potentially affecting how the town manages its beaches moving forward.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County schools earn third consecutive A rating from state
cards.teaser: The School District of Palm Beach County received an A rating from the state for the third year in a row, with 143 district-operated schools rated A or B and a record 93.5 percent graduation rate.
cards.body:
The School District of Palm Beach County earned an "A" rating from the Florida Department of Education for the third consecutive year, reflecting strong student performance across all grade levels. School districts receive letter grades based on student performance on state tests, graduation rates, and advanced coursework. This year, 143 district-operated schools, or 84 percent, were rated "A" or "B," up from 120 schools the previous year. The district set a record with a 93.5 percent graduation rate. District leaders reported that 86 percent of seniors participated in college-level coursework, including Advanced Placement, International Baccalaureate, Cambridge Advanced International Certificate of Education, or Dual Enrollment courses. Additionally, 144 recent graduates earned an associate degree alongside their high school diploma.

S.D. Spady Elementary School in Delray Beach achieved one of the district's biggest success stories, jumping from a "C" rating to an "A" rating. Principal Rona Tata, who has served 15 years as principal and five years as assistant principal, led the improvement effort. The school modified its early childhood curriculum program, which starts at age 3 and combines with kindergarten. Students who participated in the revised program are now in third grade and performing at higher levels. Spady Elementary was one of four district schools to improve from a "C" to an "A" rating this year, along with Dwight D. Eisenhower K-8, Glade View Elementary, and West Gate Elementary.

cards.headline: Boca Raton High School band to represent Florida at National Independence Day Parade
cards.teaser: The Boca Raton Community High School band will march down the National Mall in Washington D.C. on July 4 at 10:30 a.m., representing the entire state of Florida.
cards.body:
The Boca Raton Community High School band has earned a coveted spot in Washington, D.C.'s National Independence Day Parade, representing the entire state of Florida. On July 4 at 10:30 a.m., the students will march a full mile along the National Mall, from Constitution Avenue to Independence Avenue. Only bands nominated by state officials receive invitations to this prestigious event. Junior Lola Cabezas said there are millions, if not billions, of people watching. "It's a lot of pressure, but I think we'll be able to rise to the occasion," she said. Cabezas explained that marching band is physically demanding, requiring students to play, breathe, and walk while maintaining consistent sound.

Senior Stephin Restivo said the team is laser-focused on nailing every detail. "Everyone will be able to see what the Boca High band is capable of," he said. Band Director Jenn Girdlestone expressed confidence in her students. "I have full confidence in our students that they'll put their best foot forward, literally, and we'll rise to the occasion and represent our country well," she said. Senior Lily Schaffer called the opportunity amazing, noting it showcases how much the program has grown. The parade will be streamed live on YouTube for those who want to cheer on the band from home.

cards.headline: Fourth of July cookout costs rise 4 percent this year
cards.teaser: A holiday cookout meal for 10 now costs $73.82, up 4 percent from a year ago, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation's Summer Cookout Cost Survey.
cards.body:
The Fourth of July cookout tradition is getting more expensive this year. According to the American Farm Bureau Federation's Summer Cookout Cost Survey, a holiday meal for 10 people now costs $73.82, up 4 percent from a year ago. Inflation is the primary driver behind these higher costs. Ground beef prices have increased 5.5 percent, while buns are up 7.7 percent. Strawberries, damaged by a Florida frost, have seen the steepest increase at 12.4 percent. Ice cream prices have also climbed, rising 5.3 percent.

However, not all cookout staples have become more expensive. Potato prices are down this year, offering savings for those planning potato chips and salads. Corn prices have fluctuated, though locally grown corn from the Glades can provide the best deal. Budgeting expert Andrea Woroch recommends families shop strategically by comparing prices across stores to find the best deals for their grocery lists. She emphasizes that cutting down food waste is crucial, and that process begins with meal planning.

cards.headline: Breast cancer patient speaks out after Anthem denies reconstruction surgery hours before procedure
cards.teaser: Beth Clark, 48, and her surgeon are speaking out after her insurance company denied coverage for a reconstruction procedure less than 24 hours before it was scheduled.
cards.body:
Beth Clark, 48, was diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma three months ago and opted for a full double bilateral mastectomy with reconstruction. However, less than 24 hours before her reconstruction surgery, her insurance company, Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield, denied coverage for the procedure. According to her denial letter, the surgery involved a surgical mesh called GalaFlex, which Anthem determined is still considered "investigational" and lacks sufficient proof that it improves health. GalaFlex is a synthetic surgical mesh that has become controversial for breast reconstruction. While it is popular among plastic surgeons and FDA-approved for some uses in the body, it is not approved for breast reconstruction and remains an off-label, investigational, and experimental treatment. In a 2023 letter to health care providers, the FDA stated its "efficacy and safety for breast cancer patients have not been determined."

Clark's plastic surgeon, Dr. Alicia Billington, believes insurance companies should reconsider their stance. Billington uses GalaFlex mesh on most of her breast reconstruction patients and says it produces the least amount of complications compared to other options. Despite Anthem's denial, Clark underwent the reconstruction surgery with GalaFlex mesh a little more than a week ago thanks to Billington's efforts. An Anthem spokesperson stated the mesh "does not currently meet the standards required for coverage by our medical policy" without FDA approval. Clark and Billington are continuing to fight the denial, while last year Cigna became the first major insurer to approve GalaFlex for breast reconstruction.

hero.headline: Hobe Sound woman dies in home fire days before her birthday
hero.teaser: Misty Dawn White, 46, was found dead Monday after a fire broke out inside her Hobe Sound home. Friends have launched a fundraiser to help her fiance Mark rebuild.
hero.body:
Misty Dawn White, 46, was discovered dead Monday following a fire that destroyed her and her fiancé's Hobe Sound home. Authorities with the sheriff's office have identified a possible electrical issue as the cause, though the investigation remains ongoing. The loss has left her fiancé Mark and their community searching for ways to support one another through the tragedy.

Mark learned of White's death in the immediate aftermath and has since received an outpouring of support from friends and neighbors. Nina Fenn, who knew White for eight years, received a call from Mark informing her of what had happened. "It's just a terrible shame and awful loss of life," Fenn said. The community has rallied together to launch a fundraiser aimed at helping Mark rebuild and replace belongings lost in the flames. According to Fenn, the situation represents "completely a state of devastation" for everyone affected.

Those closest to White are remembering her for the meaningful impact she had on those around her. Fenn described White as a Christian woman who had a passion for gardening and plants and played the piano. "She was always the first to lend a hand," Fenn said. "She loves kids; she loves her kids. She loves people." White's willingness to help others and her genuine care for those in her life left a lasting impression on her friends and family.

The timing of White's death has compounded the grief experienced by those who loved her. White's birthday fell on the Fourth of July, meaning she died just days before turning 47. The loss is further difficult for Mark, who has already endured significant personal tragedy. Fenn explained that Mark lost his only child, Jacob, in circumstances she described as tragic. Despite these mounting losses, Fenn remains committed to supporting Mark however she can. "She's always been a good soul to me. She'll always be in our hearts," Fenn said, expressing how White's memory will continue to live on in the hearts of those who knew her.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie advances Midway Road expansion and Florida Turnpike interchange
cards.teaser: The Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of an ordinance to give 7 acres of land to FDOT to assist with a partial interchange at the Turnpike.
cards.body:
Last month, the Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of an ordinance to give 7 acres of land to the Florida Department of Transportation to assist with a partial interchange at Florida's Turnpike. Scott Samples, strategic communications manager for Port St. Lucie, noted there is a significant gap between the entrances and exits to the Turnpike currently in Port St. Lucie. Samples said the interchange is about accessibility and keeping up with growth in the city. "This is a way for us to try to accommodate the growth that's already occurred, but also the growth that will occur over the next 20 to 50 years," Samples said.

FDOT has been constructing the $95 million Midway Road Widening Project to help with congestion and safety. Crews are currently working on the first phase, widening the road from two lanes to four lanes from Selvitz Road to Jenkins Road. According to the FDOT website for the project, the second widening phase from Jenkins Road to Glades Cut Off Road is still in the design phase with construction anticipated to begin in Summer 2027. The partial interchange for the Turnpike is also still in the design phase. FDOT said the Midway Road Widening Project will also add bike and pedestrian paths, along with sidewalks. City council will vote on final approval to give the land at an upcoming meeting.

cards.headline: Glydways proposes elevated autonomous transit connecting West Palm Beach to airport
cards.teaser: A California-based autonomous transit company will present a proposal to Palm Beach County commissioners Tuesday for an elevated network of self-driving vehicles connecting downtown West Palm Beach to President Donald J. Trump International Airport.
cards.body:
Glydways, a California-based autonomous transit company with projects underway in Atlanta and California, will present its proposal to Palm Beach County commissioners Tuesday for initial consideration. The company proposes an elevated network of self-driving vehicles connecting downtown West Palm Beach to President Donald J. Trump International Airport, the convention center, Brightline and Tri-Rail stations. Senior Vice President Brian Gettinger described the concept as functioning like a "horizontal elevator," with small autonomous electric vehicles carrying four to six passengers traveling along a dedicated elevated guideway built above existing roads. The system would bypass traffic congestion, potentially cutting the trip between downtown and the airport to less than 10 minutes. Glydways estimates travel times of seven minutes or less between the convention center and airport and roughly one to two minutes between Tri-Rail and the convention center.

Gettinger said the system would cost "a small fraction" of a traditional light rail system while offering comparable passenger capacity, referencing previous South Florida light rail discussions that estimated $400 million to $500 million per mile. He emphasized the service would be priced at transit-level rates, stating "This is not a $30 ride between downtown and the airport." Tuesday's County Commission meeting will determine whether the county should formally evaluate the proposal. If commissioners move forward, the county could seek competing bids and begin deeper discussions on routes, station locations, costs and financing, with a planning and design contract potentially awarded later this year.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County deputies make 15 DUI arrests in impaired driving operation
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County sheriff's deputies targeted impaired driving ahead of the Fourth of July weekend.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County sheriff's deputies made 15 DUI arrests as part of an operation targeting impaired driving in the county. The enforcement effort came ahead of the Fourth of July weekend, a period when law enforcement agencies typically increase patrols to combat drunk driving.

The operation reflects ongoing efforts by local law enforcement to address impaired driving on Treasure Coast roads during holiday weekends when traffic and alcohol consumption typically increase.
