The All-America City Award recognizes communities that effectively bring together residents, local government, businesses and organizations to address local challenges and create meaningful, lasting change. The award has been presented annually since 1949 and is considered one of the nation's most respected civic honors. Mayor Douglas Lawson expressed pride in the recognition, saying "Little old Riviera Beach is one of the biggest, brightest, shining stars." Lawson noted that the city earned the award through long-term efforts to revitalize the community and improve residents' quality of life. Councilwoman KaShamba Miller-Anderson credited the community for the achievement, stating "This award is a tribute to the heart and determination of our residents. Every event we host, every project we complete, and every challenge we overcome happens because our community shows up for one another."

Riviera Beach's application highlighted several civic engagement programs that demonstrate the city's commitment to community participation. The Riviera Beach Youth Council involves high school students in civic leadership and advocacy work. The Citizens Leadership Academy, a civic education program, has achieved a 98 percent completion rate. The Neighborhood Reclaim Home Rehabilitation Program provides mini-grants to help longtime homeowners make necessary repairs. City leaders emphasized that these programs represent a broader commitment to treating civic engagement as an ongoing partnership between government, residents, faith groups, schools and community organizations. Miller-Anderson noted that the city is "doing a lot of innovative things to make sure that our community is able to say that they are part of what's happening here in the city."

Officials say that being named an All-America City sends a national message that Riviera Beach is a place where collaboration produces results and residents actively shape their community's future. The designation celebrates the city's progress while positioning the community for continued growth and new opportunities. Miller-Anderson added that winning this award reinforces positive momentum and brings back community pride. Other cities receiving the 2026 All-America City Award include Chelsea, Massachusetts; Franklin, Tennessee; Harlingen, Texas; Montgomery, Alabama; Morrisville, North Carolina; Norfolk, Virginia; North Charleston, South Carolina; Roanoke, Virginia; and Woodburn, Oregon.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie expands Midway Road with $95 million project, adds Florida Turnpike interchange
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie City Council approved giving 7 acres of land to the Florida Department of Transportation for a partial interchange on the Florida Turnpike as part of the Midway Road Widening Project.
cards.body:
Last month, the Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of an ordinance to give 7 acres of land to the Florida Department of Transportation to assist with a partial interchange coming to Florida's Turnpike. Scott Samples, strategic communications manager for Port St. Lucie, said the interchange is about accessibility and keeping up with growth in the city. "There's a pretty significant gap between the entrances and exits to the Turnpike currently in Port St. Lucie," Samples said. According to the FDOT website, the partial interchange is still in the design phase.

The $95 million Midway Road Widening Project is underway to help with congestion and safety. Crews are currently working on the first phase, widening the road from two lanes to four lanes from Selvitz Road to Jenkins Road. The second widening phase from Jenkins Road to Glades Cut Off Road is still in the design phase, with construction anticipated to begin in Summer 2027. FDOT is also improving the Turnpike bridge and will add bike and pedestrian paths along with sidewalks as part of the project. City council will vote on final approval to give the land at an upcoming meeting.

cards.headline: Stuart's downtown dock to close July 6 for $3 million renovation, nearly doubling slip capacity
cards.teaser: Stuart's downtown public dock will close July 6 for a $3 million renovation projected to be complete by next Fourth of July.
cards.body:
Stuart's downtown public dock will close July 6 for a $3 million renovation projected to be complete by next Fourth of July. The project will nearly double the dock's capacity, expanding from 18 to 44 slips for both motorized and non-motorized vessels. The renovation, funded by a state grant and transportation impact fees, will include a 7,500 square foot fixed dock, a 1,400 square foot floating dock and a smaller floating platform. With more than 1,400 boaters using the dock annually, Stuart Mayor Sean Reed said the upgrades serve multiple purposes beyond capacity expansion. "They're doing it to prevent storm damage during hurricanes and major storms," Reed said.

During the closure, the city is accommodating businesses and boaters who depend on the dock. Tiki Taxi & Cruises, which operates off the dock, will continue running during construction after the city allowed the company to build a gate at the end of the non-floating section for boarding. Austin Kuyrkendall, director of operations for Tiki Taxi & Cruises, acknowledged the dock's current limitations. "On the weekend that's when it can get a little hectic at the dock," Kuyrkendall said, adding that the modernization project will benefit both the city and his business.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound woman dies in home fire as community rallies to support fiance
cards.teaser: Misty Dawn White, 46, was found dead Monday after a fire broke out inside her Hobe Sound home. Preliminary findings from the sheriff's office point to an electrical issue as a possible cause.
cards.body:
Misty Dawn White, 46, of Hobe Sound, was found dead Monday after a fire broke out inside her home she shared with her fiancé Mark. Preliminary findings from the sheriff's office point to an electrical issue as a possible cause, though the fire remains under investigation. Friends have since launched a fundraiser to help Mark rebuild after the flames destroyed many of his and White's belongings.

Nina Fenn, a friend of White's for eight years, spoke about the loss and reflected on White's character. "Misty was a Christian woman. She loved gardening and plants. She plays the piano," Fenn said. "She was always the first to lend a hand. She loves kids; she loves her kids. She loves people." Fenn said the loss is compounded by grief Mark has already endured, noting he lost his one and only child, Jacob, tragically. The timing adds another layer of heartbreak, as Misty's birthday is the Fourth of July, just a few days after she passed. "She'll always be in our hearts," Fenn said.

cards.headline: Tee Box virtual golf center near Delray Beach delayed 3 months, costs $90,000 after contractor problems
cards.teaser: Tom Molen, owner of Tee Box virtual golf training center on Jog Road south of Linton Boulevard, said contractor problems delayed his opening by three months and cost him $90,000.
cards.body:
Tom Molen's dream of opening Tee Box, a virtual golf training and performance center near Delray Beach along Jog Road south of Linton Boulevard, hit significant delays and costs after contractor problems. The facility was scheduled to open in April but was postponed three months after issues with the licensed contractor hired to prepare the space. Molen said the work had to be redone, creating a costly domino effect that he estimates cost approximately $90,000. The figure doesn't include lost revenue during delays or expenses for bringing in another contractor to fix the problems. "It was double pay on a lot of things from electricians to HVAC to drywall," Molen said.

Molen worked with Code Pro of the Palm Beaches, which is warning property and business owners to thoroughly vet contractors before hiring them. Founder David Allan estimates 25% to 35% of homeowners and property owners in Palm Beach County face major issues with unvetted contractors. He recommends using Palm Beach County's online portal to verify whether contractors have proper licenses and insurance before work begins. Despite the setbacks, Molen said he is moving forward. "Like the game of golf, I gotta put that bad shot behind me," he said. Tee Box's grand opening is set for July 17.

cards.headline: Breast cancer patient denied reconstruction coverage hours before surgery despite federal law
cards.teaser: Beth Clark, 48, was denied coverage by Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield for reconstruction surgery less than 24 hours before it was scheduled, despite having invasive ductal carcinoma.
cards.body:
Beth Clark, 48, was diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma three months ago and scheduled a full double bilateral mastectomy with reconstruction. Less than 24 hours before her reconstruction surgery, her insurance company, Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield, denied coverage for the procedure. According to her denial letter, the surgery involved a surgical mesh called GalaFlex, which the insurer considered investigational with insufficient proof it improves health. GalaFlex is a synthetic surgical mesh approved by the FDA for some uses in the body but not for breast reconstruction, making it an off-label treatment. In a 2023 letter, the FDA stated that GalaFlex's "efficacy and safety for breast cancer patients have not been determined."

Dr. Alicia Billington, Clark's plastic surgeon, uses GalaFlex mesh on most of her breast reconstruction patients and says it produces the least amount of complications. Despite the denial, Clark received her reconstruction surgery with GalaFlex a little more than a week ago thanks to Billington's efforts. Last year, after investigative reporter Katie LaGrone shared breast cancer patients' denial stories in the "Patient No More" series, Cigna became the first and only major insurer to approve GalaFlex for breast reconstruction. Clark and Billington continue fighting the denial as a new bill has been introduced to modernize the Women's Health and Cancer Rights Act, a federal law protecting breast cancer patients from treatment denials.

cards.headline: Fourth of July cookout costs up 4% to $73.82 as ground beef and strawberry prices climb
cards.teaser: A Fourth of July cookout for 10 now costs $73.82, up 4% from a year ago, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation's Summer Cookout Cost Survey.
cards.body:
A Fourth of July cookout for 10 people now costs $73.82, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation's Summer Cookout Cost Survey, representing a 4% increase from a year ago. Inflation is driving the price hike, with ground beef up 5.5% and buns up 7.7%. Strawberries have been particularly hard hit by a Florida frost, climbing 12.4% in price, while ice cream prices are up 5.3%.

Some items offer relief for budget-conscious shoppers. Potato prices are down this year, benefiting those planning potato chips and salads. Corn prices have fluctuated, but locally grown corn from the Glades can provide the best value. Budgeting expert Andrea Woroch recommends comparing prices across stores to find the best deals for items on your grocery list. She emphasized that families should focus on cutting down food waste by starting with a meal plan.

hero.headline: Saint Andrew's Scots football sets sights on state title after 10-2 district championship season
hero.body:
The Saint Andrew's Scots football program is working through the summer with a clear objective: winning a state championship during the 2026 fall season. Coming off a 10-2 regular season record and a district title last year, the team's early playoff exit has fueled their ambitions for greater success. Head football coach Jimmy Robertson noted that the team's senior class provides a strong foundation for achieving that goal.

Robertson highlighted that most of the senior players are four-year veterans who came up through the middle school program. "Most of these seniors are four-year seniors. I mean, if not the majority of them came from the middle school as well. So they know how things are run. They had a lot of success in their career, and hopefully their senior year is the best season that we've had," Robertson said. This experience and continuity gives the program confidence heading into the new season.

The Scots are taking a strategic approach to improvement by scheduling tougher competition this fall. Senior Jack Williams explained the reasoning behind this decision, saying the team wants to reach the next level competitively. "We knew that we wanted to take our program to the next level. So we really have a challenging schedule for this year because we wanna compete. That's what we wanna do and we wanna take that next level, and it's by playing against really good teams that we do that and attract new people," Williams said. The more demanding slate of opponents is designed both to test the team and to put them on the map for recruits.

The players are laser-focused on one specific measure of success this season: playoff advancement. Senior Jack Whelche stressed that regular season accomplishments mean little without postseason success. "A better year is just gonna be going farther in the playoffs. Obviously we wanna go undefeated in the season, but that doesn't matter if we keep losing in the second round of the playoffs. We just gotta go farther than that, that's all that matters," Whelche said. To prepare for this push, the team is using summer workouts as both a training tool and a source of motivation. Senior Edmyer St. Jean emphasized how the daily grind contributes to the team's overall goal. "It just adds up every day as something like to look forward to. Work harder so we can see the results when we come off the season positive and break our record," St. Jean said.

cards.headline: Martin County maritime units deploy two boats with medics for Fourth of July boating weekend
cards.teaser: Martin County Maritime Response Unit will have two boats staffed with medics stationed in the north and south areas of the county as hundreds of boaters celebrate the holiday weekend on the water.
cards.body:
Hundreds of boaters are expected to hit the waterways across Florida this Fourth of July weekend. Lt. Brett Harry with Martin County Maritime Response Unit said his team will have two boats with medics on standby in Martin County's north and south regions to assist boaters. "We're just out there to mitigate anybody that needs help, whether it's something as simple as a stubbed toe to anything cardiac related, or potential spinal injuries, or anything like that," Harry said.

Boaters like Brendan and Ashley Shannon launched their boat at Sandsprit Park in Martin County on Friday with their young daughter and puppy, prioritizing safety on the water. Harry emphasized that boaters should keep their eyes on the water, have a designated driver, and pack life vests, whistles and flotation devices. "Just have fun and be safe," Harry said.

cards.headline: Martin County School Board challenges judge recommendation to reinstate teacher suspended over Charlie Kirk comments
cards.teaser: The Martin County School Board filed a court document Thursday arguing that a judge erred in recommending the reinstatement of Matt Theobald, a Spectrum Academy teacher suspended after social media comments about Charlie Kirk.
cards.body:
Matt Theobald, a social studies teacher at Spectrum Academy since 2009, was suspended last year after posting comments on social media that labeled Charlie Kirk as racist, misogynistic and a neo-Nazi. In a Thursday court filing, the Martin County School Board argued that Administrative Law Judge Jodi-Ann Vanessa Livingstone made "numerous findings" that "are not based upon competent substantial evidence" when she recommended Theobald be reinstated. The board's attorney stated that Theobald's Facebook post about Kirk was a "serious offense" and that removing him was appropriate.

Last month, Livingstone issued an order citing a recent Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal ruling that said disciplining a teacher for personal Facebook posts made off school grounds, on personal equipment, with no student involvement, violated the teacher's First Amendment rights. She also recommended Theobald be awarded back pay and benefits. According to an investigation report, Theobald admitted writing the comments about Kirk but said they were posted on his mother's private Facebook page "within a discussion among personal acquaintances" and were not intended for public view. The school board has the final say on whether Theobald gets his job back, though the timing of a final decision remains unclear.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound woman remembered after deadly home fire as community supports fiance
cards.teaser: Misty Dawn White, 46, died Monday in a home fire in Hobe Sound that preliminary findings suggest may have been caused by an electrical issue. Friends have launched a fundraiser to help her fiance Mark rebuild.
cards.body:
A Hobe Sound man is leaning on his community after losing his fiancée in a deadly home fire. Misty Dawn White, 46, was found dead Monday after a fire broke out inside the couple's home. Preliminary findings from the sheriff's office point to an electrical issue as a possible cause. The fire remains under investigation.

Nina Fenn, a friend of White's for eight years, learned of the death through a phone call from White's fiancé Mark. "It's just a terrible shame and awful loss of life," Fenn said. Friends have since launched a fundraiser to help Mark rebuild after the flames destroyed many of his and White's belongings. Fenn described the scene as completely a state of devastation. She reflected on White's character, noting she was a Christian woman who loved gardening, plants, and playing the piano and was always the first to lend a hand. The loss is compounded by grief Mark has already endured, as he lost his only child Jacob in a tragic incident. White's birthday is July 4, meaning she passed away just days before turning 47.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie advances $95 million Midway Road widening project and Florida Turnpike interchange
cards.teaser: The Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of an ordinance last month to give 7 acres of land to the Florida Department of Transportation for a partial interchange at the Florida Turnpike.
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of an ordinance last month to give 7 acres of land to the Florida Department of Transportation for a partial interchange on Florida's Turnpike. Scott Samples, strategic communications manager for Port St. Lucie, said the interchange addresses a significant gap between the entrances and exits to the Turnpike currently in the city. Samples explained that the project accommodates growth that has already occurred and growth expected over the next 20 to 50 years.

FDOT is constructing the $95 million Midway Road Widening Project to improve congestion and safety. Crews are currently working on the first phase, widening the road from two lanes to four lanes from Selvitz Road to Jenkins Road. The second widening phase from Jenkins Road to Glades Cut Off Road remains in the design phase with construction anticipated to begin in summer 2027. FDOT is also improving the Turnpike bridge and adding a partial interchange, both still in the design phase. The project will add bike and pedestrian paths along with sidewalks. City council will vote on final approval to give the land at an upcoming meeting.

cards.headline: Breast cancer patient speaks out after Anthem Blue Cross denies reconstruction surgery hours before procedure
cards.teaser: Beth Clark, 48, had her breast reconstruction surgery denied by Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield less than 24 hours before the scheduled procedure because the insurance company considers the surgical mesh GalaFlex investigational.
cards.body:
Beth Clark was diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma three months ago and chose a full double bilateral mastectomy with reconstruction. Less than 24 hours before her reconstruction surgery, her insurance company Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield denied coverage for the procedure involving GalaFlex surgical mesh, citing in her denial letter that the surgery is considered "investigational" and "there is no or not enough proof it improves health." GalaFlex is a synthetic surgical mesh approved by the FDA for some uses in the body but not approved for breast reconstruction. In a 2023 letter to health care providers, the FDA stated its "efficacy and safety for breast cancer patients have not been determined."

Dr. Alicia Billington, Clark's plastic surgeon, uses GalaFlex mesh on most of her breast reconstruction patients. While acknowledging no treatment is risk-free, Billington says the product is less risky than other options with proven success and calls it "the gold standard in breast reconstruction with implants" for many surgeons. A spokesperson for Anthem said the company regularly reviews coverage policies to ensure they are based on medical evidence and aligned with treatment standards, but noted that without FDA approval, the mesh does not meet the company's medical policy standards for coverage. Despite the denial, Clark received her reconstruction surgery with the GalaFlex mesh a little more than a week ago after Billington found a mechanism to make it happen. Both Clark and Billington are continuing to fight the denial.

cards.headline: Lantana veteran gets lien removed and roof repaired after contractor issues
cards.teaser: Stephen McCoy, a disabled and retired veteran in Lantana, had a nearly $7,000 lien placed on his home after his roofing contractor allegedly failed to pay for materials, but the lien was lifted after WPTV contacted the company.
cards.body:
Stephen McCoy, a disabled and retired veteran from Lantana, hired Seabreeze Roofing and Sheet Metal in Boynton Beach to replace his nearly 20-year-old roof before hurricane season. McCoy made six payments totaling more than $17,000 to the company but said they left two holes unfinished on the back of his home and stopped responding to his calls, texts and emails starting in January. Letters from Gulfeagle Supply warned that the company had filed a nearly $7,000 lien on his home, claiming the materials supplier was not paid for supplies furnished to Seabreeze Roofing for McCoy's property.

After WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey spoke with the owner of Seabreeze Roofing, a final waiver of lien signed by Gulfeagle Supply and notarized was delivered to McCoy within an hour, removing the lien from his home. The contractor also sent workers back to complete the two unfinished roof repairs. McCoy said he felt like crying when the issue was resolved after months of frustration and worry about potentially needing to hire an attorney or go to court.

hero.headline: North Palm Beach celebrates Fourth of July with fireworks and America 250 events at country club
hero.teaser: North Palm Beach residents and visitors will celebrate Independence Day with a full day of activities, live entertainment and fireworks at North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse on July 4.
hero.body:
The free community event includes a pool party, lawn games, live music, a barbecue buffet and a fireworks finale scheduled for 9 p.m. Organizers say this years event also recognizes Americas 250th anniversary, bringing an added sense of celebration to the annual holiday tradition in Palm Beach County.

The festivities begin with a community pool party from 11 a.m. at the country club pool area. Guests can enjoy a water slide, DJ entertainment, games and activities, food and beverages and a poolside satellite bar. Beginning at 4:30 p.m., families can take part in activities including cornhole, Connect 4, giant Jenga, face painting and lawn games. Live music from Solstice Reign is expected to begin around 6 p.m.

Ashley Shipman, director of parks and recreation, said the golf course will offer one of the best locations to watch the fireworks display. The Clubhouse will also host a Fourth of July barbecue buffet from 4:30 p.m.

cards.headline: Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach offers sea turtle nesting season programs through September
cards.body:
Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach is offering educational and interactive programs during peak sea turtle nesting season through September. Guests can participate in guided Turtle Walks, the Hatchling Discovery Program, Hatchling Releases, Tidal Tots and Plastic Free July Community Action Day. According to the center, these programs are designed to give visitors an opportunity to learn more about sea turtle conservation along one of the world's busiest sea turtle nesting beaches.

The Turtle Walk program allows participants to observe the nesting process while learning about sea turtle biology, conservation and ongoing research efforts. Educational demonstrations may include the use of red-light headlamps, amber lighting, night scopes and research tag scanning equipment. The center's education and research departments work together during nesting season to collect and analyze data related to nesting activity and hatchling success. Sea turtle nesting season in Florida typically runs from March through October. Conservation groups continue encouraging beachgoers to turn off beachfront lighting at night, properly dispose of trash and avoid disturbing nesting turtles or hatchlings. Registration information and program details are available through Loggerhead Marinelife Center.

hero.headline: Florida advances plan to bar undocumented students from state colleges and adult education programs
hero.body:
Florida's State Board of Education has voted to move forward with rules that would prevent undocumented students from enrolling in the state's 28 community colleges and adult education programs. The restrictions would also apply to GED preparation courses, which many students use as a pathway to college or workforce training. This action builds on an earlier decision by Florida's university system Board of Governors, which approved plans to ban undocumented students from the state's more competitive public universities starting in the 2027-28 academic year. Students already enrolled would not be affected by the university proposal.

Those supporting the restrictions contend that taxpayer-funded educational institutions should serve only students who are legally present in the United States. However, immigrant advocates and students have objected strongly to the policy. Alexander Vallejos, a student with DACA protection, argued that Florida is closing opportunities for young people who have lived their entire lives in the state and attended Florida schools. Vallejos stated, "We're just asking for an opportunity to earn our future through education. Because when Dreamers succeed, Florida succeeds." These new restrictions follow Florida's previous decision to eliminate in-state tuition rates for many undocumented students, including those protected under DACA.

The same week, Governor Ron DeSantis began implementing a new state law that enables Florida to designate organizations as terrorist groups. The law, which took effect July 1, allows the governor and Florida Cabinet to make designations based on recommendations from state domestic security officials. DeSantis announced that Florida will seek to designate the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the Muslim Brotherhood, and Antifa, in addition to more than 90 organizations already designated as terrorist groups by the federal government. These federal designations include cartel-connected groups and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

If the Cabinet approves these designations, the state could block taxpayer funding, contracts, and other public support for the listed organizations. The law also imposes penalties for providing material support to designated groups and could allow for dissolution of some organizations under state law. CAIR and civil rights groups immediately filed lawsuits in federal court challenging the designations as unconstitutional. According to a statement from the Southern Poverty Law Center's deputy legal director Scott McCoy, "Gov. DeSantis does not have the power to unilaterally brand an organization with this vilifying designation and punish those who support it without due process or judicial review." Supporters of the law argue that Florida is taking necessary steps to combat extremism and protect public institutions.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds reports raising more than $90 million as Florida GOP governor's race intensifies
cards.teaser: U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds' campaign and affiliated political committee say they have now raised more than $90 million this cycle, including more than $23 million in the second quarter.
cards.body:
Byron Donalds, the front-runner in the GOP race to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis, entered the week with mounting signs of momentum. His campaign and affiliated political committee have raised more than $90 million this cycle, including more than $23 million in the second quarter. The campaign recently launched a $20 million statewide advertising buy, putting Donalds on television as Florida's August primary approaches. Donalds picked up endorsements from Attorney General James Uthmeier and Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia, both statewide officials appointed by DeSantis. He also has backing from the two incoming legislative leaders, Senate President Jim Boyd and House Speaker Sam Garrison. The endorsements are notable in a primary where DeSantis himself has not endorsed a successor, though several figures connected to his administration have lined up behind Donalds.

While Donalds builds money and institutional support, Lt. Gov. Jay Collins filed a lawsuit this week challenging another Republican candidate, James Fishback, arguing he does not meet Florida's constitutional requirement that a governor live in the state for at least seven years before being elected. The legal complaint points to Fishback's ties to Washington, D.C., including allegations that he claimed a D.C. property as a primary residence and voted there in 2020. Fishback has denied the allegations, arguing he was born and raised in Florida and accusing Collins of trying to damage his campaign. The court fight adds another layer of uncertainty to the GOP primary, with mail ballots soon going out and the Aug. 18 primary approaching.

cards.headline: Gov. DeSantis allies accuse Lt. Gov. Jay Collins' wife of running anonymous social media accounts critical of the governor
cards.teaser: Multiple X accounts were suddenly deactivated after allegations they were tied to Layla Collins, wife of Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, in accusations that came from prominent veterans of Gov. Ron DeSantis' communications team.
cards.body:
Multiple X accounts were suddenly deactivated after allegations emerged they were tied to Layla Collins, wife of Lt. Gov. Jay Collins. Christina Pushaw, a communications specialist in the Governor's Office, and Jeremy Redfern, Deputy Chief of Staff to Attorney General James Uthmeier, both pointed at online sleuthing tying accounts to the Second Lady. Pushaw shared information posted by Promota CEO Robert Salvador that showed the account @FSUdude01670 appeared connected to a phone number similar to a known number and email used by Layla Collins. Florida Politics obtained screenshots verifying this through two-factor authentication, which can be triggered when an individual tries to gain access to an account without the preset password or if the social platform deems the password has been compromised.

Pushaw also identified a second account, @bobnamy1, that she said appeared tied to Layla Collins. Pushaw noted that the account content was entirely comprised of promoting Jay Collins and attacking people who did not endorse him, including the governor. Redfern joined in with criticism, stating "The FSUDude account was tied directly to her personal cell phone number." After Pushaw and Redfern leveled their criticisms publicly, both accounts were deactivated. Both Pushaw and Redfern previously served as Press Secretaries for DeSantis. Redfern now works for Uthmeier, who has endorsed U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds for Governor.

cards.headline: St. Petersburg unveils $8.1 billion plan to transform Tropicana Field site into mixed-use district
cards.teaser: A new civic park, a permanent home for The Woodson African American Museum of Florida, and thousands of income-restricted housing units sit at the center of The Burg Bid's vision for redeveloping Tropicana Field and the surrounding Historic Gas Plant District.
cards.body:
St. Petersburg Mayor Ken Welch has selected The Burg Bid as the city's preferred plan to redevelop Tropicana Field and surrounding land. Led by Blake Investment Partners and Related Group, the $8.1 billion proposal would transform stadium parking and public land into a mixed-use district featuring housing, hotels, offices, retail, cultural institutions, workforce training, public art and entertainment space. The team would purchase 58 acres of city-owned land for $275 million, with the full land package valued at $405 million including $130 million in land the city would retain. A $20 million deposit would be required when a purchase and sale agreement is executed.

The district would center on Samuel Davis Park, a 13-acre civic and cultural space within 18.5 acres of total public park space. The park would include The Woodson African American Museum of Florida, a Museum of Public Art, a Discovery Center, event lawns, playground, splash pad, and concert lawn. The proposal calls for 3,600 income-restricted housing units over 15 years, with 1,800 units in the Historic Gas Plant District and 1,800 on complementary sites elsewhere in St. Petersburg. Development would occur in three phases of approximately five years each. Phase 1 would establish cultural and workforce anchors including the Woodson, the Collaboratorium workforce training center, the Legacy Link pedestrian corridor, and a multimodal transportation hub. The team's lease with the city ends after the 2028 season.

cards.headline: Florida Secretary of State asks court to keep Republican candidate Paula Stark off the ballot after missing filing deadline
cards.teaser: Secretary of State Cord Byrd is asking the courts to keep Stark off the ballot as he sought to cast doubt on her claims about an alleged paperwork mix-up that ended up disqualifying her.
cards.body:
Paula Stark's incomplete qualifying materials were timestamped less than 30 minutes before the noon deadline on June 12, and she is now suing to get on the ballot. In the Secretary of State's response to her Leon Circuit Court lawsuit, Secretary of State Cord Byrd is asking courts to keep Stark off the ballot. Five state employees gave sworn written court declarations stating that Stark's treasurer and partner, Joel Davis, never submitted the crucial Form 6 nor was it accidentally handed back when he submitted the rest of the paperwork in the final hour of the qualifying window. Form 6 is a public disclosure of financial interests. Byrd argued that had Stark or Davis "exercised the slightest degree of care or prudence" by questioning why the Form 6 was allegedly handed back, "the mistake would have been discovered" while Davis was at the Division.

Three weeks after the qualifying deadline passed, Stark still hasn't submitted Form 6, said Election Records Division Bureau Chief Erica Ikay Reeve in a court disclosure. Stark was one of 12 candidates who didn't properly turn in Form 6, with half of them correcting the problems and still qualifying. Reeve also cited additional issues: Davis filed a campaign finance report over one month late, reported excessive contributions, and has an incorrect address on file. The state revoked Stark's Friends of Paula political committee in November over $16,000 in unpaid fines from missed campaign finance deadlines. If Stark is removed from the ballot, the August Primary for House District 47 would feature only Democrats Jorge Figueroa and Anthony Nieves, benefiting Florida Democrats in this traditionally blue district representing Osceola and Orange counties.

hero.headline: Hobe Sound woman dies in home fire days before her birthday
hero.teaser: Friends are rallying around a Hobe Sound man who lost his fiancée in a deadly house fire Monday, with the tragedy coming just days before her birthday on the Fourth of July.
hero.body:
Misty Dawn White, 46, died Monday after a fire broke out inside her home in Hobe Sound. She was found at the scene after flames engulfed the residence. The sheriff's office has indicated that an electrical issue may have caused the fire, though the investigation remains ongoing.

Mark, White's fiancé, learned the devastating news and has since received support from his community. Friends have established a fundraiser to help him rebuild after the fire destroyed many of his and White's belongings. Nina Fenn, who had been friends with White for eight years, described the aftermath as "completely a state of devastation." Fenn spoke exclusively about the tragedy and visited the scene in the days following the fire to process her grief.

Fenn reflected on White's character and the kind of person she was to those around her. "Misty was a Christian woman. She loved gardening and plants. She plays the piano," Fenn said. "She was always the first to lend a hand. She loves kids; she loves her kids. She loves people." White's death carries additional sadness given the grief Mark was already carrying. Fenn explained that Mark had previously lost his only child, Jacob, in a tragedy. The loss of White compounds the pain Mark has already endured, and Fenn has been working to support him during this difficult time.

The timing of White's death adds another layer of heartbreak for those who knew her well. White's birthday is July Fourth, meaning she passed away just days before turning a year older. Fenn emphasized that White's memory will remain with those who loved her. "She's always been a good soul to me. She'll always be in our hearts," Fenn said. As the community continues to rally around Mark, White is being remembered for her generous spirit and the positive impact she had on the people in her life.

cards.headline: Martin County maritime teams deploy medics for Fourth of July boating safety
cards.teaser: Martin County Maritime Response Unit is deploying two boats with medics on standby in the northern and southern parts of the county as hundreds of boaters take .
cards.body:
Hundreds of boaters are hitting waterways across Florida to celebrate the Fourth of July weekend. Martin County Maritime Response Unit is deploying two boats with medics on standby in the northern and southern parts of the county to assist boaters during the holiday. Lt. Brett Harry said his team expects hundreds of boaters to be on the water celebrating this weekend.

The maritime response team will handle medical situations ranging from minor injuries like stubbed toes to serious conditions including cardiac events and potential spinal injuries. Harry urged boaters to keep their eyes on the water, have a designated driver, and pack life vests, whistles and flotation devices. Among those taking to the water Friday was the Shannon family, who launched from Sandsprit Park in Martin County with their young daughter and puppy. "Just have fun and be safe," Harry said.

cards.headline: Martin County School Board fights judge's order to reinstate teacher suspended over Charlie Kirk post
cards.teaser: The Martin County School Board is challenging an administrative law judge's recommendation to reinstate a Spectrum Academy teacher who was suspended for calling Charlie Kirk racist and a neo-Nazi on Facebook.
cards.body:
Matt Theobald, a social studies teacher at Spectrum Academy since 2009, sparked controversy with social media comments labeling Charlie Kirk as racist, misogynistic and a neo-Nazi. In a Thursday court filing, the Martin County School Board argued Administrative Law Judge Jodi-Ann Vanessa Livingstone erred in recommending Theobald's reinstatement, saying "numerous findings ... are not based upon competent substantial evidence." The board's attorney claims Theobald's Facebook post about Kirk was a "serious offense" and removing him was appropriate.

In an order issued last month, Livingstone cited a recent Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal ruling that said disciplining a teacher for personal Facebook posts made off school grounds, on personal equipment, with no student involvement, violated the teacher's First Amendment rights. The judge also recommended Theobald be awarded back pay and benefits. According to an investigation report, Theobald admitted writing the comments about Kirk but said they were posted on his mother's private Facebook page "within a discussion among personal acquaintances" and were not intended for public view.

hero.headline: Body of missing diver recovered near Fort Pierce Inlet
hero.teaser: Deputies report that the body of a missing diver was found on the Florida coast near Fort Pierce Inlet.
hero.body:
The body of a missing diver was discovered on the Florida coast near Fort Pierce Inlet, according to deputies. The recovery was made after the diver was reported missing.

St. Lucie County deputies are handling the investigation. Authorities have not released the identity of the diver or circumstances surrounding the incident.

cards.headline: Driver held Port St. Lucie teens at gunpoint after Orbeez pellet shooting incident
cards.teaser: A driver held teenagers at gunpoint after they shot Orbeez pellets at his car in Port St. Lucie, police say.
cards.body:
Police in Port St. Lucie responded to an incident where a driver held teenagers at gunpoint after they shot Orbeez pellets at his vehicle. The confrontation occurred after the teens targeted the driver's car with the gel pellets.

Port St. Lucie police are investigating the incident. Details about potential charges or the identities of those involved have not been released.

cards.headline: Two people rescued after boat sinks in St. Lucie County Intracoastal Waterway
cards.teaser: Two people were rescued after their boat sank in the Intracoastal Waterway in St. Lucie County.
cards.body:
Rescue crews responded to the Intracoastal Waterway in St. Lucie County after a boat sank. Two people who were aboard the vessel were rescued from the water.

Body camera footage captured the rescue operation. Authorities have not released information about what caused the boat to sink or the condition of those rescued.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie approves land transfer for new Florida Turnpike interchange at Midway Road
cards.teaser: The Port St.
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of an ordinance last month to transfer 7 acres of land to the Florida Department of Transportation for a partial interchange at Florida's Turnpike. Scott Samples, strategic communications manager for Port St. Lucie, said the interchange addresses a significant gap between current Turnpike entrances and exits in the city. According to Samples, the project is designed to improve accessibility and accommodate growth over the next 20 to 50 years.

FDOT is constructing the $95 million Midway Road Widening Project to address congestion and safety. The first phase is widening the road from two lanes to four lanes between Selvitz Road and Jenkins Road. The second widening phase from Jenkins Road to Glades Cut Off Road is in the design phase, with construction anticipated to begin in Summer 2027. The partial interchange remains in the design phase. The project will also add bike and pedestrian paths along with sidewalks. Port St. Lucie resident Erin Scheumeister acknowledged the construction is annoying but necessary, saying the road expansion will make it easier to get to work. City council will vote on final approval to transfer the land at an upcoming meeting.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce woman recognized for supporting little free libraries
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce woman received recognition for her support of little free libraries in the community.
cards.body:
A woman from Fort Pierce was recognized for her contributions to supporting little free libraries. The acknowledgment highlights her efforts to promote community reading and book access.

Little free libraries are neighborhood book exchanges where residents can take or leave books. The recognition came from local organizations supporting literacy initiatives.

cards.headline: Legacy Lions Football standings updated for Port St. Lucie team
cards.teaser: Sports Illustrated published updated standings for the Legacy Lions Football team in Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
The Legacy Lions Football team from Port St. Lucie had its standings updated in Sports Illustrated. The publication tracks high school football teams across the state.

The Legacy Lions compete in Port St. Lucie area high school football. Standings are regularly updated throughout the football season to track team performance.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce property at 629 Salisbury Circle listed on real estate market
cards.teaser: A residential property at 629 Salisbury Circle in Fort Pierce is available on the real estate market.
cards.body:
The property at 629 Salisbury Circle in Fort Pierce is listed on Realtor.com. The listing appeared on the real estate platform for prospective buyers to view.

The address is located in Fort Pierce's 34982 ZIP code area. Details about the property are available through the Realtor.com listing platform.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast travel writer names favorite town after 20 years of Florida visits
hero.body:
A travel writer who has visited Florida for more than 20 years has identified a Treasure Coast town as a personal favorite, citing its lively arts scene and uncrowded beaches. The endorsement appears in Travel + Leisure magazine.

The article highlights the town's combination of cultural offerings and beach access that sets it apart from more crowded Florida destinations. The writer emphasized the arts scene as a particular draw alongside the beaches.

The recognition comes as the Treasure Coast continues to attract visitors seeking alternatives to busier coastal areas in South Florida. The region encompasses Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties along Florida's Atlantic coast.

The full article detailing the writer's experiences and specific recommendations for the town appears in Travel + Leisure. The piece is part of ongoing travel coverage highlighting lesser-known Florida destinations.

cards.headline: Fourth of July cookout costs up 4 percent in Florida
cards.teaser: A holiday meal for 10 now costs $73.82, up 4 percent from last year, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation's Summer Cookout Cost Survey.
cards.body:
A Fourth of July cookout for 10 people will cost $73.82 this year, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation's Summer Cookout Cost Survey. That represents a 4 percent increase from last year. Inflation is driving up prices across the board. Ground beef costs are up 5.5 percent, while buns have increased 7.7 percent. Strawberries, affected by a Florida frost, have seen the steepest increase at 12.4 percent. Ice cream prices are up 5.3 percent.

Not all cookout staples are more expensive. Potato prices have declined this year, offering savings for those planning potato salads or chips. Corn prices have fluctuated, though locally grown corn from the Glades can provide the best value. Budgeting expert Andrea Woroch recommends several strategies to manage costs. She suggests comparing prices across stores, identifying which retailers offer the best deals for items on your shopping list. Woroch also emphasized that meal planning is essential for families looking to control spending, particularly by cutting down on food waste.

cards.headline: Saint Andrew's Scots football targets state title after 10-2 season
cards.teaser: The Saint Andrew's Scots finished last season with a 10-2 record and a district title, but a second-round playoff exit left the team wanting more.
cards.body:
The Saint Andrew's Scots finished last season with a 10-2 record and a district title, but a second-round playoff exit has the team focused on a state title run this fall. Head football coach Jimmy Robertson said most of the seniors are four-year players, with many coming from the middle school program. "Most of these seniors are four-year seniors. I mean, if not the majority of them came from the middle school as well. So they know how things are run. They had a lot of success in their career, and hopefully their senior year is the best season that we've had," Robertson said.

To compete at the next level, the Scots have scheduled more challenging opponents for the 2026 fall football season. Senior Jack Williams said playing stronger teams will help the program advance. "We knew that we wanted to take our program to the next level. So we really have a challenging schedule for this year because we wanna compete," Williams said. Senior Jack Whelche emphasized that advancing further in the playoffs is the priority. "A better year is just gonna be going farther in the playoffs. Obviously we wanna go undefeated in the season, but that doesn't matter if we keep losing in the second round of the playoffs," Whelche said. Senior Edmyer St. Jean said summer workouts are building momentum for the season ahead.

cards.headline: Boca Raton High School band marches in National Independence Day Parade
cards.teaser: The Boca Raton Community High School band will represent Florida at the National Independence Day Parade in Washington, D.C. on July 4.
cards.body:
The Boca Raton Community High School band has earned a spot in Washington, D.C.'s National Independence Day Parade, representing the entire state of Florida. On July 4 at 10:30 a.m., the students will march a full mile along the National Mall, from Constitution Avenue to Independence Avenue. Only bands nominated by state officials receive invitations to this prestigious event.

Junior Lola Cabezas said millions, if not billions, of people will be watching. "It's a lot of pressure, but I think we'll be able to rise to the occasion," she said. Senior Stephin Restivo said the team is laser-focused on nailing every detail, emphasizing the importance of marching and timing so everyone can see what the band is capable of. Band Director Jenn Girdlestone said she has full confidence the students will represent their country well. Senior Lily Schaffer said making it to Washington, D.C. proves how much the program has grown. The parade will be streamed live on YouTube for those who want to watch from home.

cards.headline: Riviera Beach named only Florida city to win 2026 All-America City Award
cards.teaser: Riviera Beach was named one of just 10 communities in the U.S. to receive the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League.
cards.body:
Riviera Beach has been named one of 10 U.S. communities to receive the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League, making it the only Florida city selected for the honor this year. The prestigious award recognizes communities that bring residents, local government, businesses and organizations together to solve local challenges and create lasting change. The announcement came during the National Civic League conference in Denver, where Riviera Beach leaders presented the city's efforts to strengthen community engagement. Mayor Douglas Lawson called the recognition a proud moment for the city, saying "Little old Riviera Beach is one of the biggest, brightest, shining stars." Lawson said the city earned the award through a long-term effort to revitalize Riviera Beach and improve quality of life for residents.

Riviera Beach's application highlighted several civic engagement programs, including the Riviera Beach Youth Council, which involves high school students in civic leadership and advocacy, the Citizens Leadership Academy with a 98 percent completion rate, and the Neighborhood Reclaim Home Rehabilitation Program, which provides mini-grants to help longtime homeowners make critical repairs. Councilwoman KaShamba Miller-Anderson credited residents for the honor, stating "This award is a tribute to the heart and determination of our residents." The All-America City Award has been presented annually since 1949 and is considered one of the nation's most respected civic honors.

cards.headline: Juno Beach residents want fence reinstalled at JB-7 beach access point
cards.teaser: Residents at the Colony Condos say people using the JB-7 public walkway are cutting through their private property since the town removed the old fence in 2023.
cards.body:
Residents at the Colony Condos say people using the JB-7 public walkway are cutting through their private property since the town removed the old fence in 2023 for safety reasons. Lori Hill, a Colony resident, said the problem peaks in summer, with beachgoers parking in private spots and pushing through bushes with coolers, fishing rods and lawn chairs. Hill said residents previously confronted trespassers directly but now call police instead after encountering rude responses. Without the fence, only bushes separate the public access path from private land.

The dispute came before the Juno Beach Town Council at a recent meeting, where a town official noted the town is not obligated to install a fence. Vice Mayor Pro Tem DD Halpern suggested exploring a lower-cost solution, saying "I understand fencing is expensive, but I'd like to see maybe we can help them with a lower-cost fence or some combination of split rail and shrubs." Not all beachgoers report issues. Michael House, who walks to JB-7 from a public lot a couple of blocks away, said he has not witnessed the problems residents describe. The council agreed to take up the fence question during its upcoming budget discussions on July 15.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County schools earn third consecutive A rating from state
cards.teaser: The School District of Palm Beach County received an A rating from the state for the third year in a row.
cards.body:
For the third consecutive year, the School District of Palm Beach County earned an "A" rating from the Florida Department of Education. This year, 143 district-operated schools, or 84 percent, received A or B ratings, up from 120 schools the previous year. The district achieved a record-setting 93.5 percent graduation rate, and district leaders reported that 86 percent of seniors participated in college-level coursework, including Advanced Placement, International Baccalaureate, Cambridge Advanced International Certificate of Education, or Dual Enrollment courses. Additionally, 144 recent graduates earned an associate degree alongside their high school diploma.

One of the district's biggest success stories came from S.D. Spady Elementary School in Delray Beach, which jumped from a C rating to an A this year. Principal Rona Tata, who has served 15 years as principal and five years as assistant principal, led the turnaround effort. Three years ago, staff began modifying the early childhood curriculum program, which starts at age 3 and combines with kindergarten. Many of those students are now in third grade and performing at higher levels. Spady Elementary was one of four district schools to improve from a C to an A rating this year, along with Dwight D. Eisenhower K-8, Glade View Elementary, and West Gate Elementary.
